definition: A curatorial lens for watches traditionally proportioned, styled, or marketed for men—without prescribing who may wear them.
history: Pocket-watch movements migrated to the wrist in the early twentieth century, and practical military designs helped normalize the wristwatch for men. Modern collections now range from discreet dress pieces to expressive technical instruments.

definition: A curatorial lens spanning jewelry-led, classically proportioned, and technically ambitious watches associated with women's collections.
history: Decorative wristwatches appeared for women before the wristwatch became a universal daily object. Contemporary women's watchmaking combines gem-setting and design craft with the same mechanical complications found across haute horlogerie.

definition: An independent Vallée de Joux manufacture known for high complications and the architectural language of the Royal Oak.
history: Jules Louis Audemars and Edward Auguste Piguet established their workshop in 1875. The maison paired traditional complicated movements with a radical steel luxury-watch vocabulary that reshaped the category in the 1970s.

definition: A contemporary fashion house extending its urban design language into accessible, trend-driven timepieces.
history: Established as the youthful expression of Giorgio Armani, the label translated its streetwise aesthetic into watches that balance fashion and function.

definition: A German fashion house whose watches combine sharp tailoring codes with modern, business-ready design.

definition: A British heritage house whose watches reflect classic trench codes and check-pattern sophistication.
history: Burberry translated its iconic outerwear heritage into timepieces that balance classic British style with modern runway influences.

history: Founded in 1847, Cartier helped make the wristwatch a modern design object through early twentieth-century forms such as the Santos and Tank. Its watchmaking balances recognizable geometry with specialist métiers.

definition: A rotating carriage that carries the escapement and balance, averaging positional errors through continuous motion.
history: Conceived for pocket watches around the turn of the nineteenth century, the tourbillon addressed the long periods those watches spent upright. In wristwatches it is as much a demonstration of construction and finishing as a precision strategy.

definition: A mechanism that starts, stops, and resets an independently driven seconds display to measure elapsed time.
history: Early chronographs served scientific, sporting, and industrial timing. Wristwatch versions evolved from single-pusher layouts to two-pusher, flyback, split-seconds, and high-frequency configurations.

definition: A calendar mechanism programmed to distinguish month lengths and leap years without routine date correction.
history: The logic was proven in clocks and pocket watches before becoming one of the defining wristwatch complications of the twentieth century. Traditional mechanisms are mechanically encoded for the Gregorian four-year cycle.

definition: An on-demand acoustic complication that strikes the current hours, quarter-hours, and remaining minutes.
history: Repeating mechanisms let owners read time in darkness before electric light. Miniaturizing their racks, snails, hammers, and gongs for the wrist made the minute repeater a summit of acoustic watchmaking.

definition: A poetic astronomical display that tracks the visible progression of the lunar cycle through a dial aperture or rotating indication.
history: Lunar displays descend from astronomical clocks and later appeared in portable watches. Modern versions range from familiar 59-tooth mechanisms to high-accuracy systems requiring correction only after many generations.

definition: The regulating interface that releases the gear train in measured steps while returning energy to the oscillator.
history: Successive escapement designs made portable timekeeping more durable and precise. The Swiss lever became dominant, while detent, co-axial, and experimental direct-impulse systems pursue different balances of efficiency and stability.

definition: The oscillating wheel that, together with its hairspring, forms the timekeeping heart of a mechanical watch.
history: The balance replaced earlier foliot regulators in portable timekeepers. Temperature compensation, improved alloys, free-sprung adjustment, and silicon components have steadily refined its consistency.

definition: A mechanical calibre whose mainspring is wound by a weighted rotor responding to the wearer's motion.
history: Self-winding wristwatches matured in the early twentieth century as compact rotor and bumper systems became practical. Bidirectional winding and efficient bearing systems later made automatic construction an everyday standard.

definition: The duration a fully wound mechanical watch can continue running, or the display that indicates its remaining stored energy.
history: Long-running marine chronometers made stored-energy awareness operationally important. Wristwatch indicators later turned the same information into a useful and visually expressive complication.

definition: A watch whose dial and movement bridges are opened to reveal the structure and motion of the calibre.
history: Openworked watchmaking developed from decorative piercing and engraving that exposed a mechanism without sacrificing its stability. Contemporary skeleton designs may begin as transformed calibres or be engineered around transparency from the outset.

definition: A watch that integrates several demanding complication families—typically calendar, timing, and chiming functions—within one coherent movement.
history: The tradition began with highly commissioned pocket watches that condensed astronomical, acoustic, and chronographic mechanisms. Wristwatch grand complications require extraordinary packaging, energy management, and assembly discipline.
